hypothesis: Glycyl-L-leucine (Gly-Leu, KEGG C02155) is increased/characteristic in 12-month-old infants receiving dairy-based complementary protein relative to meat-based complementary protein.
rationale: Searches located no primary study reporting glycyl-L-leucine (glycylleucine, HMDB0000759 / KEGG C02155) as differentially abundant between dairy-based and meat-based complementary feeding in infants, in either biofluid or stool. The one directly on-point human infant study design I found (Nutrients 2021 serum metabolomics of the 5-12 mo meat- vs dairy-based controlled-feeding trial, and the companion growth/microbiome RCT) matches the exposure and age window exactly, but nothing in the retrieved abstracts/records indicated glycylleucine or dipeptides among the discriminating metabolites, so it cannot be counted as direct support. What I did find is only generic, pathway-level plausibility: (i) Glycyl-L-leucine is catalogued as a bovine milk constituent in the Milk Composition Database (BMDB0000759), consistent with dairy foods delivering this dipeptide directly; (ii) reviews of milk protein-derived peptides document that dipeptides from casein/whey digestion appear in plasma after dairy protein ingestion, with dipeptides more bioavailable than longer peptides. Countervailing generic evidence: a controlled crossover meal trial in healthy adults comparing fermented dairy with red meat found dipeptides on BOTH sides of the comparison - hydroxyproline-containing dipeptides (plus carnosine, taurine, creatine) as meat biomarkers and proline-based dipeptides as novel putative dairy biomarkers - i.e., 'dipeptide' abundance per se does not cleanly favour dairy, and Gly-Leu specifically was not named as a dairy marker. Because relevant literature exists but never addresses this feature+group combination and the class-level signal is mixed, this is weak (score 1) rather than 0 (nothing found) or -1 (direct opposite-direction finding).

evidence.title: Different Blood Metabolomics Profiles in Infants Consuming a Meat- or Dairy-Based Complementary Diet
evidence.study_population: Formula-fed US infants in a controlled feeding trial consuming meat- vs dairy-based complementary foods from 5 to 12 months, followed to 24 months; targeted and untargeted serum metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Exactly the exposure/age context of the hypothesis, showing that meat vs dairy complementary protein produces distinguishable metabolomic profiles; however the retrieved record gives no indication that glycyl-L-leucine (or dipeptides generally) was among the dairy-associated discriminants, so it supports plausibility of a diet-driven signal but not this specific feature or direction.

evidence.title: Milk Composition Database: metabocard for Glycyl-L-leucine (BMDB0000759)
evidence.study_population: Bovine milk composition reference database (not a human study)
evidence.relevance: Documents Glycyl-L-leucine as a compound catalogued in milk, providing a direct dietary-exposure route by which dairy-based complementary foods could raise this dipeptide; database-level (not primary-study) evidence only.

evidence.title: Bioavailability of milk protein-derived bioactive peptides: a glycaemic management perspective (Nutrition Research Reviews)
evidence.study_population: Review of human and in vitro studies of whey/casein protein ingestion in adults
evidence.relevance: Notes that plasma dipeptide levels exceed tripeptide levels after whey ingestion and lists specific branched-chain dipeptides released from whey hydrolysates, supporting the general mechanism that dairy protein intake elevates small dipeptides - but no data on Gly-Leu or on infants.

evidence.title: Metabolomics-based biomarkers of fermented dairy and red meat intake: a randomized controlled trial in healthy adults
evidence.study_population: Healthy adults, randomized controlled postprandial meal trial (fermented dairy vs red meat)
evidence.relevance: Class-level evidence that dipeptides discriminate dairy from meat intake in both directions: hydroxyproline-based dipeptides/carnosine mark meat while proline-based dipeptides are putative dairy markers; glycylleucine is not identified as a dairy marker, so this tempers rather than supports the specific hypothesis.

evidence.title: A meat- or dairy-based complementary diet leads to distinct growth patterns in formula-fed infants: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.study_population: Formula-fed infants randomized to meat- vs dairy-based complementary diets from ~5 to 12 months
evidence.relevance: Establishes that the meat vs dairy complementary-protein contrast at 12 months is a real, well-characterized exposure with differing protein/amino-acid intakes, but reports growth outcomes rather than dipeptide metabolites.

evidence.title: glycylleucine (Wikidata Q27140595)
evidence.relevance: Confirms identifier mapping for the queried feature (CAS 869-19-2, KEGG C02155, HMDB0000759, ChEBI 73514), validating that searches targeted the correct compound; no biological association data.

contradicting_evidence: No study reported glycyl-L-leucine higher in meat-fed infants, so there is no direct contradiction. However, the adult dairy-vs-red-meat biomarker RCT indicates that meat intake also generates characteristic dipeptides (hydroxyproline-containing dipeptides, carnosine/anserine-type compounds), so dipeptide elevation is not specific to dairy; this makes the class-level rationale ambiguous rather than opposing.

caveats: The feature label 'Glycyl-L-leucine Esi-3.5' is an untargeted LC-MS annotation (ESI mode, retention-time tag) and dipeptide isomers/isobars (e.g. Leu-Gly, other Gly-X/X-Gly pairs, or leucine+glycine adducts) are notoriously hard to resolve, so annotation confidence itself is a limitation. Dipeptides in stool/serum also arise from host and microbial proteolysis of any dietary protein, from mucin and endogenous protein turnover, and are sensitive to peptidase (e.g. DPP-4, aminopeptidase) activity and to sample handling, meaning any dairy-vs-meat difference could reflect total protein load or fermentation intensity rather than dairy protein per se. Additional caveats: search coverage was truncated (server tool-use limit reached before the final planned queries on Gly-Leu content in milk vs beef), full texts and supplementary metabolite tables of the meat-vs-dairy infant trial were not retrievable within this session, and that trial measured serum rather than fecal metabolites, so a null there would not exclude a fecal effect.
